greek: Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis praeter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre universorum. Nec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quae ipse apud se praefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: It was not angels, therefore, who made us, nor who formed us, neither had angels power to make an image of God, nor any one else, except the Word of the Lord, nor any Power remotely distant from the Father of all things. For God did not stand in need of these [beings], in order to the accomplishing of what He had Himself determined with Himself beforehand should be done, as if He did not possess His own hands. For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 213 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 437 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, were always present with God and by them, as his hands, he made all things.
limits: 'Manus' (hands) is an image of God acting directly; the text states presence and agency, not an explicit doctrine of equality. Harvey's note 5 (p. 213) cross-refers to Haer. 5.1 for 'Filium et Spiritum Sanctum Dei manus' (not read here). The sentence does not exclude an instrumental reading of Word and Wisdom, which opponents use. Harvey prints 'preefinierat' (OCR; variant note 4 prefers 'praefinierat').

greek: Bene autem et in prophetis Malachias ait: Nonne unus Deus qui constituit nos? Nonne Pater unus est omnium nostrum? Consequenter autem et Apostolus ait: [Unus] Deus, inquit, Pater, qui super omnes, et in omnibus nobis. Similiter autem et Dominus: Omnia mihi, inquit, tradita sunt a Patre meo; manifeste ab eo qui omnia fecit: non enim aliena, sed sua tradidit ei.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: Rightly also has Malachi said among the prophets: Is it not one God who has established us? Have we not all one Father? Malachi 2:10 In accordance with this, too, does the apostle say, There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and in us all. Ephesians 4:6 Likewise does the Lord also say: All things are delivered to Me by My Father; Matthew 11:27 manifestly by Him who made all things; for He did not deliver to Him the things of another, but His own.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 214 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 438 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: There is one God, the Father, who is above all and in us all; the Son says all things are delivered to him by the Father, who made all things.
limits: 'Pater, qui super omnes' (Eph 4:6) is the phrase Unitarians cite as 'Father above all'. The text contrasts nothing with the Son or Spirit; the same paragraph calls the Father 'in us all'. The brief's '4.20.5-6 Father is above all' is wrong: the phrase is at 4.20.2 only (negative for 4.20.5-6). Harvey's footnote (p. 214, '* Athanas. de Decret. syn. Nic.') marks Athanasius as a parallel for the next sentence (creation 'ex eo quod non erat'); not read.

greek: Et quoniam Verbum, id est Filius, semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Quoniam autem et Sapientia, quae est Spiritus, erat apud eum ante omnem constitutionem, per Salomonem ait: Deus sapientia fundavit terram, paravit autem coelum prudentia. Sensu ejus abyssi eruperunt, nubes autem manaverunt ros.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation, He declares by Solomon: God by Wisdom founded the earth, and by understanding has He established the heaven. By His knowledge the depths burst forth, and the clouds dropped down the dew. Proverbs 3:19-20
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 214 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 438 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: Irenaeus says the Word (the Son) and Wisdom (which is the Spirit) were both with the Father before all creation.
limits: The identification 'Wisdom which is the Spirit' is Irenaeus's own in this chapter; in 4.20.4 'by the Word and Wisdom' the two are not identified. It states pre-creation presence (before all creation) but not consubstantiality or the Spirit's divinity in these words. Opponents may read the Wisdom=Spirit equation, with Prov 8:22, as making the Spirit a created instrument of creation.

greek: Et rursus autem: Dominus creavit me principium viarum suarum in opera sua, ante saecula fundavit me, in initio antequam terram faceret, priusquam abyssos constitueret, et priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, antequam montes confirmarentur: ante omnes autem colles genuit me. Et iterum: Cum pararet coelum, eram cum illo, et cum firmos faceret fontes abyssi, quando fortia faciebat fundamenta terrae, eram apud eum aptans. Ego eram cui adgaudebat, quotidie autem laetabar ante faciem ejus in omni tempore, cum laetaretur orbe perfecto, et jocundaretur in filiis hominum.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: And again: The Lord created me the beginning of His ways in His work: He set me up from everlasting, in the beginning, before He made the earth, before He established the depths, and before the fountains of waters gushed forth; before the mountains were made strong, and before all the hills, He brought me forth. And again: When He prepared the heaven, I was with Him, and when He established the fountains of the deep; when He made the foundations of the earth strong, I was with Him preparing [them]. I was He in whom He rejoiced, and throughout all time I was daily glad before His face, when He rejoiced at the completion of the world, and was delighted in the sons of men. Proverbs 8:27-31
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 214-215 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 438 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: Irenaeus quotes Prov 8:22-31 ('the Lord created me ... brought me forth'), applying it to Wisdom, which he calls the Spirit.
limits: Latin verb is 'creavit me' (Prov 8:22 as quoted, LXX-type text); the final verb 'genuit me' (v. 25) is translated 'brought me forth' by ANF. Harvey's note 7 (p. 214) says this text 'gave great confidence to the Arian party in the fourth century'. Irenaeus does not comment on 'creavit' here; his gloss is 'before all creation' and Wisdom = Spirit (item 3). The Greek of the quotation in Harvey's margin is not legible in the OCR (the verb cannot be read reliably). Harvey's note on Hebrew qanah ('possession by parental generation', p. 215) is Harvey's own, not Irenaeus's.

greek: Unus igitur Deus, qui Verbo et Sapientia fecit et adaptavit omnia: hic est autem Demiurgus, qui et mundum hunc attribuit humano generi, qui secundum magnitudinem quidem ignotus est omnibus his qui ab eo facti sunt: nemo enim investigavit altitudinem ejus, nec veterum qui quieverunt, nec eorum qui nunc sunt, secundum autem dilectionem cognoscitur semper per eum, per quem constituit omnia. Est autem hic Verbum ejus Dominus noster Jesus Christus.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: There is therefore one God, who by the Word and Wisdom created and arranged all things; but this is the Creator (Demiurge) who has granted this world to the human race, and who, as regards His greatness, is indeed unknown to all who have been made by Him (for no man has searched out His height, either among the ancients who have gone to their rest, or any of those who are now alive); but as regards His love, He is always known through Him by whose means He ordained all things. Now this is His Word, our Lord Jesus Christ
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 215 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 438 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: There is one God, who made all things by the Word and Wisdom; he is unknown in greatness and known in love through his Word, Christ Jesus.
limits: 'Demiurgus' is used positively for the one Creator God, which Gnostic-language critics will note; the Spirit is not named here. The sentence ties the Creator to his Word, Jesus Christ, but does not formulate a Trinity. Latin 'adaptavit' (Voss. 'aptavit' variant, Harvey note).

greek: Haec prophetice significabant prophetae, sed non quemadmodum quidam dicunt, invisibili Patre omnium exsistente, alterum esse eum, qui a prophetis videretur. Sed secundum magnitudinem quidem ejus, et mirabilem gloriam, nemo videbit Deum, et vivet; incapabilis enim Pater: secundum autem dilectionem et humanitatem ... Potens est enim in omnibus Deus: visus quidem tunc per Spiritum prophetice, visus autem et per Filium adoptive, videbitur autem et in Regno coelorum paternaliter, Spiritu quidem praeparante hominem in Filium Dei, Filio autem adducente ad Patrem, Patre autem incorruptelam donante in aeternam vitam, quae unicuique evenit ex eo quod videat Deum.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: These things did the prophets set forth in a prophetical manner; but they did not, as some allege, [proclaim] that He who was seen by the prophets was a different [God], the Father of all being invisible. ... But in respect to His greatness, and His wonderful glory, no man shall see God and live, for the Father is incomprehensible; but in regard to His love, and kindness, and as to His infinite power, even this He grants to those who love Him ... For God is powerful in all things, having been seen at that time indeed, prophetically through the Spirit, and seen, too, adoptively through the Son; and He shall also be seen paternally in the kingdom of heaven, the Spirit truly preparing man in the Son of God, and the Son leading him to the Father, while the Father, too, confers [upon him] incorruption for eternal life, which comes to every one from the fact of his seeing God.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 216 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 439 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: The Father is invisible and incomprehensible, yet seen through the Spirit, the Son and in the kingdom: the Spirit prepares man, the Son leads him, the Father gives incorruption.
limits: Answers the claim that the God seen by the prophets is a different, invisible Father: the Father is incomprehensible yet is seen through the Spirit, the Son and the paternal kingdom. The order Spirit -> Son -> Father (prepares, leads, gives incorruption) is an economic sequence that Unitarians read as hierarchy; the text itself makes the Father the giver. Latin 'exsistente' and 'preeparante' are OCR-normalised; ellipses are in the source.

greek: Et homines igitur videbunt Deum, ut vivant, per visionem immortales facti et pertingentes usque in Deum. Quod, sicut praedixi, per prophetas figuraliter manifestabatur, quoniam videbitur Deus ab hominibus qui portant Spiritum ejus, et semper adventum ejus sustinent. Quemadmodum et in Deuteronomio Moses ait: In die ista videbimus, quoniam loquetur Deus ad hominem, et vivet.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: Men therefore shall see God, that they may live, being made immortal by that sight, and attaining even unto God; which, as I have already said, was declared figuratively by the prophets, that God should be seen by men who bear His Spirit [in them], and do always wait patiently for His coming. As also Moses says in Deuteronomy, We shall see in that day that God will talk to man, and he shall live.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 217 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 439 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: Men shall see God and live, as the prophets foretold, because God is seen by those who bear his Spirit.
limits: Weak support only: 'Deus' is the subject of 'videbitur', and the Spirit appears as 'His Spirit' (Spiritus ejus, dwelling in the seer) without an explicit statement of the Spirit's divinity. Read with item 6, the Father is seen through the Son and the Spirit.

greek: Quidam enim eorum videbant Spiritum propheticum ... Sic igitur manifestabatur Deus: per omnia enim [OCR 'shee', unresolved] Deus Pater ostenditur, Spiritu quidem operante, Filio vero administrante, Patre vero comprobante, homine vero consummato ad salutem.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: Thus, therefore, was God revealed; for God the Father is shown forth through all these [operations], the Spirit indeed working, and the Son ministering, while the Father was approving, and man's salvation being accomplished.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 218 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 439 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: God the Father is revealed through the Spirit working, the Son administering, and the Father approving.
limits: The sentence gives an operational triad: Spirit working, Son administering, Father approving, man saved. Harvey's apparatus records 'ministrante' (Clermont, Voss.) and 'consummante' (AR.) as variants for 'administrante'; the unresolved OCR word ('shee') is probably a particle, not read. Unitarians read the ordering as hierarchy (Son as a servant-minister). The Latin 'Spiritu operante' attributes the working to the Spirit, not to the Father.

greek: Enarrat ergo ab initio Filius Patris, quippe qui ab initio est cum Patre, qui et visiones propheticas, et divisiones charismatum, et ministeria sua, et Patris glorificationem consequenter et composite ostenderit humano generi, apto tempore ad utilitatem. Ubi est enim consequentia, illic et constantia: et ubi constantia, illic et pro tempore: et ubi pro tempore, illic et utilitas: et propterea Verbum dispensator paternae gratiae factus est ad utilitatem hominum.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: Therefore the Son of the Father declares [Him] from the beginning, inasmuch as He was with the Father from the beginning, who did also show to the human race prophetic visions, and diversities of gifts, and His own ministrations, and the glory of the Father, in regular order and connection, at the fitting time for the benefit [of mankind]. For where there is a regular succession, there is also fixedness; and where fixedness, there suitability to the period; and where suitability, there also utility. And for this reason did the Word become the dispenser of the paternal grace for the benefit of men, for whom He made such great dispensations, revealing God indeed to men, but presenting man to God, and preserving at the same time the invisibility of the Father
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 219 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 439 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: The Son has been with the Father from the beginning and declares him; yet the Word 'became' the dispenser of the Father's grace for men.
limits: 'Verbum ... factus est' ('the Word became the dispenser') is the phrase Unitarians cite against an eternal Word; the same sentence says the Son 'is with the Father from the beginning'. ANF's 'preserving the invisibility of the Father' is cited from the ANF text; the Latin of that clause was not read on the page.

greek: Gentes quidem primo catechizabat Apostolus, quemadmodum in eo libro, qui ante hunc est, ostendimus, discedere ab idolorum superstitione, et unum Deum colere, factorem coeli et terrae, et universae conditionis fabricatorem: esse autem hujus Filium Verbum ejus, per quem constituit omnia, et hunc in novissimo tempore hominem in hominibus factum, reformasse quidem humanum genus, destruxisse autem et devicisse inimicum hominis, et donasse suo plasmati adversus reluctantem victoriam.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: As I have pointed out in the preceding book, the apostle did, in the first place, instruct the Gentiles to depart from the superstition of idols, and to worship one God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and the Framer of the whole creation; and that His Son was His Word, by whom He founded all things; and that He, in the last times, was made a man among men; that He reformed the human race, but destroyed and conquered the enemy of man, and gave to His handiwork victory against the adversary.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 232 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 445 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: Irenaeus says the Son is the Word by whom God founded all things, and who was made a man in the last times.
limits: The Son is the Word 'by whom He founded all things': agency in creation is attributed to the Son, the Word. No statement on eternal generation or on the Spirit in this paragraph. Harvey's note 8 (p. 232, on 24.2) cites Ignatius, Ad Polycarpum, as an echo; Greek not read in the source.

greek: esse autem unum Deum, qui est super omnem principatum, et dominationem, et potestatem, et omne nomen quod nominatur: et hujus Verbum, naturaliter quidem invisibilem, palpabilem et visibilem in hominibus factum, et usque ad mortem descendisse, mortem autem crucis.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: and that there is one God, who is above all principality, and dominion, and power, and every name which is named; Ephesians 1:21 and that His Word, invisible by nature, was made palpable and visible among men, and did descend to death, even the death of the cross; Philippians 2:8
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 232 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 445 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: There is one God above all, and his Word, invisible by nature, became visible among men and died on the cross.
limits: 'Verbum ... naturaliter invisibilem' says the Word is invisible by nature (the Father is 'above all' by Eph 1:21, as in item 2). The Word's visibility is by incarnation; the text does not explain the relation of Word to Father in being. Harvey's footnote 8 (p. 232) cites Ignatius, Ad Polycarpum (Greek 'tov aoraton', 'tov apathe') as an echo; Greek not checked in the source.

greek: Quemadmodum enim in novo Testamento ea quae est ad Deum fides hominum aucta est, additamentum accipiens Filium Dei, ut et homo fieret particeps Dei ... cum sit unus et idem Deus Pater et Verbum ejus, semper assistens humano generi, variis quidem dispositionibus, et multa operans, et salvans ab initio eos qui salvantur.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: For as, in the New Testament, that faith of men [to be placed] in God has been increased, receiving in addition [to what was already revealed] the Son of God, that man too might be a partaker of God; ... since there is one and the same God the Father, and His Word, who has been always present with the human race, by means indeed of various dispensations, and has wrought out many things, and saved from the beginning those who are saved
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 245 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 451 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: There is one and the same God, the Father and his Word, always present with mankind across both Testaments.
limits: 'Unus et idem Deus Pater et Verbum ejus' (one and the same God, the Father and his Word) states the unity of God and Word across both Testaments. It says nothing of the Spirit. The Word here is 'the Word of God' and could be read by Unitarians as a divine speech/act; the sentence's logic is about judgement and salvation, not the Word's ontology.

ref: 4.33.7 (modern division; the creed sentence is the second part of 33.7)

limits: Rule-of-faith sentence: 'sententia firma, quae est in Spiritu Dei' (firm belief in the Spirit of God); the Spirit 'sets forth the dispensations of the Father and the Son'. The Spirit is not called God in this sentence, and 'Spiritus Dei' could be read as an agency; the Spirit is parallel to the Father and Son as the one who reveals. translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.

what_it_says: The spiritual man knows always the same God, the same Word of God, and the same Spirit of God, who was poured out in the last times.
limits: 'Eundem Deum ... eundem Verbum Dei ... eundem Spiritum Dei' (the same God, the same Word of God, the same Spirit of God) is the closest Book IV statement to a Trinitarian triad. It says the three are 'the same' in identity across time, not that they are one God in three persons; the Spirit is said to be 'poured out' in the last times (ANF bracket '[knowing that He descends]' is ANF's, not in the Latin).

greek: Et eundem hunc patremfamilias, aliquando quidem mittentem servos, aliquando quidem Filium suum. A quo igitur Patre missus est Filius ad eos colonos, qui interfecerunt eum, ab hoc et servi. ... Quem igitur illi Dominum praedicabant incredulis, hunc Christus tradidit his qui obediunt Ei: et qui priores, sive primum per servilem legislationem, vocaverat Deus, hic posteriores, sive postea per adoptionem assumsit. Plantavit enim Deus vineam humani generis, primo quidem per plasmationem Adae, et electionem patrum ...

For God planted the vineyard of the human race when at the first He formed Adam and chose the fathers
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.

what_it_says: The householder (God the Father) sent his son to the vineyard; the God who called the fathers is the same God who sent the Son.
limits: Hard passage for subordination: the Son is 'missus' (sent) by the Father in the parable ('A quo igitur Patre missus est Filius'; Harvey's Latin, section 1). The text's argument is the unity of 'the God who called' both dispensations ('unus et idem Deus Pater', Latin p. 278). Latin 'tradidit' is rendered 'teach' by ANF. The sending language is what opponents cite; this passage does not give a doctrine of the Son's origin.

greek: Lac vobis potum dedi non escam: nondum enim poteratis escam percipere; id est, eum quidem adventum Domini, quem secundum hominem, didicistis; nondum autem Patris Spiritus requiescit super vos, propter vestram infirmitatem ... Et propter hoc coinfantiatum est homini Verbum Dei cum esset perfectus, non propter se, sed propter hominis infantiam sic capax effectus, quemadmodum homo illum capere potuit.

It was for this reason that the Son of God, although He was perfect, passed through the state of infancy in common with the rest of mankind, partaking of it thus not for His own benefit, but for that of the infantile stage of man's existence, in order that man might be able to receive Him.

what_it_says: The Son, though perfect, took the stage of infancy for man's sake so that man could receive him; the Spirit of the Father had not yet rested on the Corinthians.
limits: The Son 'was perfect' yet 'passed through infancy' for man's sake, so that man could receive him: the answer to 'growth/ignorance of the Son'. The Spirit is 'Spiritus Patris' (of the Father) not yet resting on the Corinthians. OCR of 'coinfantiatum' (Latin word) is uncertain; the printed Latin reads as given. The Latin reads 'Verbum Dei cum esset perfectus' (the Word of God), while ANF renders 'the Son of God': a translation choice that bears on the Son's identity.

greek: Patre quidem bene sentiente, et jubente; Filio vero ministrante, et formante; Spiritu vero nutriente, et augente; homine vero paulatim proficiente, et perveniente ad perfectum, id est, proximum infecto fieri.

what_it_says: The Father plans and commands, the Son works and forms, the Spirit nourishes and increases; man, created, grows toward the uncreated God.
limits: A three-part work: Father plans and commands, Son ministers and forms, Spirit nourishes and increases. Operational, not ontological. 'Infectus' (uncreated, unbegotten) is Irenaeus's Latin term; Harvey's margin gives a Greek parallel (ayevyrov / Greek 'Patre ... Spiritu' OCR only). Unitarians cite 'Son ministering' and 'Spirit increasing' as subordinate roles; Trinitarians read it as one operation distributed. Harvey's margin cross-refers to Gr. and Massuet, not read in full.

greek: Et sic principalitatem quidem habebit in omnibus Deus, quoniam et solus infectus, et prior omnium, et omnibus, ut sint, ipse est causa: reliqua vero omnia in subjectione manent Dei. ... Perfectus enim est infectus: hic autem est Deus.
greek_edition: W. W. Harvey (ed.), Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy, archive.org 10606565bsb). Latin text read from the PDF text layer (pdftotext); OCR, ligatures normalised; bracketed or unresolved OCR marked. Harvey's margin and footnote Greek parallels are not part of the quote.
english: And thus in all things God has the pre-eminence, who alone is uncreated, the first of all things, and the primary cause of the existence of all, while all other things remain under God's subjection. ... For the Uncreated is perfect, that is, God.
translator: English: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1; Book IV by W. H. Rambaut). Latin: own transcription of Harvey's text.
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2 p. 296 (Latin); ANF vol. 1 (1885) p. 471 (English; page from OCR page markers, not checked on the image)
edition: Harvey 1857 vol. 2; Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, eds. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe; Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent text; archive.org antenicenefather0001unse_s4g9 OCR)
what_it_says: God alone is uncreated, the first of all things and the primary cause of existence; the uncreated is perfect, that is God.
limits: 'Solus infectus' ('alone uncreated') is the sentence Unitarians cite: if only the Father is uncreated, the Son and Spirit are created. The text says the Father is 'the first of all things' and 'primary cause', and that the uncreated is God; it does not name the Son or Spirit as created. The sentence is in a passage on the growth of man; Harvey's margin and apparatus are not decisive. Scholarly replies (e.g. Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, cited by Harvey; not read here) are not contained in this sentence.

greek: Si igitur tradideris ei quod est tuum, id est, fidem in eum et subjectionem, recipies ejus artem, et eris perfectum opus Dei. Si autem non credideris ei, et fugeris manus ejus, erit causa imperfectionis in te qui non obedisti, sed non in illo qui vocavit. Ille enim misit, qui vocarent ad nuptias; qui autem non obedierunt ei, semetipsos privaverunt regia coena.

For He commissioned [messengers] to call people to the marriage, but they who did not obey Him deprived themselves of the royal supper. Matthew 22:3, etc.

what_it_says: If you do not believe and flee his hands, the imperfection is yours, not God's; God's skill is not defective.
limits: The 'hands' here are the Maker's (manus ejus, the Creator's), not the Son and Spirit; the Trinitarian content is nil. Use only to show that 4.39 has no Son/Spirit doctrine in this passage; the answer is that imperfection comes from disobedience, not from God's skill ('ars Dei non deficit').
